title: Latency‑first shard merging with token‑aware fallback for rerank endpoint
creator: Ava Martínez
description:
Goal: Reduce 95th/99th percentile tail latency for the rerank endpoint while preserving or improving quality for short‑to‑medium candidate lists (<=128 tokens per candidate). Approach: implement a latency‑first 'shard merge' path that attempts parallel scoring across multiple microshards, but merges partial results early when downstream token budgets/timeouts risk breaching SLOs. If a shard cannot finish within a configured soft deadline, its partial score will be estimated using a lightweight fallback (cached embedding similarity or first‑pass logistic proxy) so the system can return a ranked result instead of blocking on slow kernels.

Motivation and tradeoffs:
- Current problem: long tail caused by a few slow candidates (long context, heavy KV cache misses, or GPU kernel variability) blocks the entire batch. Conservative timeouts hurt quality; aggressive timeouts drop candidates and lower recall.
- Latency‑first merge: prioritizes meeting endpoint latency SLOs by merging early and using fallbacks where necessary. Tradeoff is potential small, controlled degradation in rank quality for rare slow candidates versus large improvements in overall latency and perceived availability.
- Fallback strategies considered: (1) cached vector similarity (very fast, modest fidelity), (2) small quantized model sketch (offloaded to CPU/GPU tiny model), (3) logistic/regression proxy trained on historic features (cache-miss, candidate length, model variance). We selected (1) + (3) combined for an ensemble fallback: cached similarity if embedding exists, else regression estimate.

Design summary:
- Request routing: incoming rerank requests are sliced into N microshards based on candidate count and token budgets; shards are dispatched in parallel to the scorer pool.
- Soft deadline per shard: default = min(ceil(SLO_fraction * request_SLO), token_budget_based_deadline). If a shard does not respond by soft deadline, return partial scores + fallback estimates for remaining candidates.
- Merge semantics: partial scores are normalized by shard-level calibration factors before merge. Calibration factors are periodically recomputed via background calibration jobs using recent ground-truth rerank labels.
- Token accounting: enforce per-request token ceiling; shards report token consumption early so scheduler can deprioritize heavy shards mid-flight.
- Observability: add metrics for fallback_rate, fallback_type, shard_latency_distribution, partial_merge_count, normalized_score_drift, and per-model calibration_offset. Create alert if fallback_rate > 2% for >= 10m.

Acceptance criteria (measurable):
- 95th percentile latency reduction >= 25% on production rerank traffic (baseline: last 7d) for median candidate sizes
- 99th percentile latency reduction >= 15%
- Quality regression: NDCG@10 drop <= 0.8% measured on daily canary eval set
- Fallback rate < 3% on canary traffic and <5% in real production for first 48h rollout

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Design sketch + config knobs (DONE: design doc link).  Estimated 1 sprint.
2) Scheduler changes: implement shard creation, token accounting, per‑shard soft deadlines, and early reporting. 2 sprints.
3) Fallback service: small read‑only cache lookup + regression estimator service with simple HTTP RPC. 1 sprint.
4) Merge node changes: normalize partial scores, run ensemble fallback insertion, produce final ranking. 1 sprint.
5) Canary rollout: feature flagged by customer/route; run canary at 1% then ramp. Monitor quality and latency dashboards. 1 sprint.

Progress / current state:
- Design doc created: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RERANK/Shard+Merge+Latency+First (internal)
- Prototype (scheduler + soft deadline hooks) merged to feature branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/10233
- Local perf results (synthetic load): 95p latency -27%; 99p -12% with fallback_rate ~1.1% using default knobs.
- Added metrics in internal instrumentation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/445
- Regression estimator prototype trained on historical rerank logs (small logistic model) and tested against canary set — AUC stable, NDCG impact estimated 0.4% relative drop when used as only fallback; ensemble with cached similarity reduces impact to 0.15%.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Default soft deadline formula: conservative vs aggressive. Proposal: default = min(0.65 * request_SLO, token_budget_deadline). Under review by SRE.
- Calibration cadence: hourly vs every 10 minutes. Decided: start hourly, monitor drift.
- Memory pressure on scorer pool when adding early reporting code path: need microbenchmarking.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: fallback introduces bias on rare candidate types (e.g., very long docs). Mitigation: record detailed telemetry and add per-customer opt-out flag for fallback; also provide a strict SLO path (no fallbacks) for enterprise/dedicated customers.
- Risk: regression estimator cold‑start. Mitigation: warm it using synthetic labeled pairs; fallback to cached similarity when estimator confidence low.

Rollout plan and monitoring:
- Canary: start with internal traffic -> canary routes (1% of traffic) for 24h with automated rollback if fallback_rate > 5% or NDCG@10 drop > 1.2%.
- Ramp to 10% for 48h if stable, then to 50% and GA after 7d of stable telemetry.
- Dashboards: rerank/latency/95/99, rerank/fallback_rate, rerank/ndcg_canary, rerank/normalized_score_drift.

Next engineering tasks (assigned):
- Rohan: finalize scheduler soft deadline knobs and implement shard early reporting (ETA: 2026-03-18).
- Mei Chen: finalize regression estimator API and add confidence score (ETA: 2026-03-10, prototyped).
- SRE: review canary auto‑rollback thresholds and alerting (contact: Jonah Reeves).

Notes for reviewers: please pay attention to the calibration transform applied in merge_node.normalize_scores; numeric stability edge cases were observed for extreme score distributions. Also verify we use the planned per‑model calibration table rather than global scalar during the first rollout to avoid systematic shifts.
